The consumer of this output has no mechanism for distinguishing what was found from what was generated. This paper formalizes the problem as narrative completion under uncertainty and advances a falsifiable hypothesis: that the fused stream is nonetheless separable, because the boundary between evidential grounding and generative interpolation is geometrically decidable from transformer hidden states and the intensity of interpolation is quantifiable along a continuous gradient. The proposed instrument is a synesthetic provenance decomposition in which an auxiliary classification head, running parallel to the primary language modeling head, projects the shared hidden-state representations onto a continuous provenance gradient at every token position. Drawing on the linear representation hypothesis and the approximate orthogonality of semantic subspaces in highdimensional transformer embeddings, the paper proposes that provenance attributes are recoverable from the residual stream without distorting the geometry on which the primary unembedding head depends. The architecture produces a three-channel continuous signal analogous to RGB color depth, decomposing each token's generation into retrieval-grounded (R), parametric-memory (G), and generative-interpolative (B) components. The paper connects this decomposition to directed persistent path-homology and the complement set formalism for measuring structured absence, argues that the boundary between measurement and generation in LLM output is a continuous gradient rather than a discrete threshold, presents falsification protocols including dimensionality reduction stress tests against Cover's theorem, and specifies a concrete experimental protocol for empirical validation including ground-truth labeling pipelines, ablation study designs, and proposed benchmark datasets. The central empirical prediction is the confident-interpolation signature: high interpolation magnitude coexisting with low output entropy. If the signature is recoverable from the hidden state and survives the falsification battery, the architecture is a detector of structural confabulation, the failure entropy-based tools cannot see because they read low entropy as grounding.\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7612142\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.21203/rs.3.rs-8589677/v1\", \"title\": [\"Self-Aware Language Models: A Taxonomy and Evaluation of Epistemic Uncertainty and Hallucination Mitigation\"], \"abstract\": \"Abstract\\n

Artificial intelligence is rapidly getting ubiquitous, getting intertwined with people's everyday lives. As the adoption grows, so does the need to verify large language models (LLMs) for correctness. The inability of LLMs to recognize their own knowledge gaps remains a fundamental limitation. While prior research address subsets of these mechanisms, they do not analyze them explicitly as manifestations of epistemic self-awareness nor research their interaction as a unified capability. In this review we investigate knowledge gap awareness, an emerging field that seeks to enable LLMs with epistemic self-awareness to detect, present and respond to the absence of knowledge. We synthesize research across five key mechanisms: (i) reflective prompting, (ii) uncertainty quantification, (iii) selective prediction and abstention, (iv) retrieval-based verification, and (v)confidence calibration. Drawing on 51 curated papers using PRISMA methodology, we provide a comprehensive taxonomy, evaluate current benchmarks, and analyze practical applications in medicine, science, education, law, and collaborative AI. We also outline open challenges and limitations in modeling epistemic context-drive knowledge gap monitoring in LLMs and its applications in read world.
